messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 77

He sits on the edge of the couch, knees pressed together, feet flat against the floor. At forty-one, his body still carries the long, lean architecture of a dancer, but the muscles in his shoulders remain permanently wound. When our office clock ticks, his eyes flick to the door. He maps every exit, every blind spot in the room, the way he once mapped stage directions. His story begins years earlier, in a country that no longer appears on most humanitarian maps. He leaves his village in Southeast Asia to volunteer with a medical relief organization, moving between forward camps and makeshift clinics across a fractured region. The heat presses down like a physical weight. The smell of diesel and cordite clings to his clothes long after he showers. He works eighteen-hour days, triaging children with compound fractures, wrapping tourniquets with hands that will later tremble at a coffee cup. He does not notice the slow fraying. He only notices it when the relief plane touches down and he steps onto home soil. The transition is not a landing but a collapse. What follows is a pattern he recognizes but cannot interrupt. Nights begin with the ceiling fan slicing the dark. At 2:14 a.m., his chest tightens. He does not dream so much as relive. The sound of a distant generator becomes an artillery barrage. He wakes drenched, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he is back in the triage tent. When his wife reaches for him, he flinches before he can stop himself. He apologizes, but the distance between them in the bed feels like a fault line. He is a dancer by profession, or he was. His company rehearses contemporary pieces that demand precision, breath, and trust in his partners. Now, when he stands in rehearsal, his body betrays him. A sudden clap from the wings sends his shoulders hiking toward his ears. He loses his rhythm, his gaze dropping to the floorboards as if scanning for debris. He stops attending rehearsals, citing a knee injury, though the pain remains entirely in the space between his shoulder blades. He tells his wife he needs to rest, but he is afraid of stillness. In stillness, the images rise unbidden: a tarp stretched over three bodies, the precise angle of a shattered femur, the silence that follows a medevac chopper. He avoids the news. He stops driving past the river district where the aid convoy once passes. He cancels dinners with old friends because he cannot bear the casual way they laugh, the unburdened ease of conversation. When he tries to speak of it, the words fracture. He says he feels like a ghost haunting his own life. His marriage strains under the weight of his withdrawal. His wife leaves warm meals on the counter. He eats them cold, staring at the steam as it fades, wondering why his body no longer recognizes peace. In our sessions, he speaks in careful, measured sentences, as if each syllable must be placed precisely. He describes how his hands shake when he pours tea. How he checks the gas stove six times before leaving the house. How he sleeps on the guest side of the bed, back against the wall, eyes open to the room. He does not ask for relief. He asks only to understand why his own nervous system has become a battlefield. I listen as he maps the terrain of his fear, noting the way his jaw tightens when he mentions the children he cannot save, the way his breath shallows when he describes the sound of a dropping curtain. He remains here, in this chair, speaking what he cannot carry alone.
